hoses: 5-inch LDH supply line from hydrant outlet to Engine 181 intake
200-foot 1¾-inch attack line from Engine 181 pump panel discharge to front door
sceneElements.elevation: Grade-level entry unless otherwise stated in a problem

problems.title: Pump Discharge Pressure
problems.question: Engine 181 is supplying one 200 ft 1¾-inch attack line flowing 185 GPM through a ChiefXD 185 fog nozzle at 50 PSI. Use C = 15.5, no elevation, and no appliance loss. What pump discharge pressure is required?
formulaBreakdown: PP = FL + NP + elevation + appliance loss.
FL = C × (GPM / 100)^2 × hose length in hundreds.
Round FL to nearest 5 PSI: 105 PSI.
problems.instructorExplanation: The attack line friction loss rounds to 105 PSI. Adding the 50 PSI nozzle pressure gives a required pump discharge pressure of 155 PSI.
problems.explainMistake: A common mistake is stopping at friction loss only. Pump discharge pressure must include nozzle pressure after friction loss is calculated.

problems.title: Attack Line Friction Loss
problems.question: The attack line is 200 ft of 1¾-inch hose flowing 185 GPM. Using C = 15.5, how much friction loss is present in the attack line?
formulaBreakdown: FL = C × (GPM / 100)^2 × hose length in hundreds.
problems.instructorExplanation: Using the 1¾-inch hose coefficient and listed flow, the attack-line friction loss is 106.1 PSI, rounded to 105 PSI.
problems.explainMistake: Do not add nozzle pressure when the question asks only for friction loss.

problems.title: Hydrant Pressure Drop
problems.question: The hydrant static pressure is 70 PSI and residual pressure is 60 PSI while supplying one 185 GPM attack line. Use the scenario's hydrant pressure-drop chart: pressure drop % = (static - residual) ÷ static × 100. Chart: 0-10% drop = 3 more equivalent lines, 10-15% = 2, 15-25% = 1, over 25% = 0. How many additional equivalent 185 GPM attack lines does this chart indicate?
formulaBreakdown: Using the chart stated in this scenario, 10-15% drop corresponds to 2 additional equivalent lines.
problems.instructorExplanation: The scenario's chart maps a 14.3% pressure drop to two additional equivalent lines. This is a chart-reading training question, not an NFPA 291 available-flow projection.
problems.explainMistake: Do not use the raw 10 PSI pressure difference as 10%. Divide by static pressure to obtain 14.3%.

problems.title: Extended Attack Line Pump Discharge Pressure
problems.question: The original attack line is 200 ft of 1¾-inch hose flowing 185 GPM at 50 PSI. If the line is extended by two additional 50 ft sections, the total length becomes 300 ft. Use C = 15.5, no elevation, and no appliance loss. What pump discharge pressure is required?
formulaBreakdown: Round FL to nearest 5 PSI: 160 PSI.
problems.instructorExplanation: Adding 100 ft increases the friction loss enough to require a pump setting of about 210 PSI.
problems.explainMistake: Recalculate friction loss using the full 300 ft length.

problems.title: Second-Floor Attack Line Pump Discharge Pressure
problems.question: The same 200 ft 1¾-inch ChiefXD 185 attack line is moved to a second-floor fire area. The nozzle flows 185 GPM at 50 PSI. Use C = 15.5 and, for this training problem, add 5 PSI elevation for the stated one-floor rise. No appliance loss. What pump discharge pressure is required?
formulaBreakdown: PP = FL + NP + elevation + appliance loss.
problems.instructorExplanation: Moving the same line to the second floor adds the stated 5 PSI training elevation allowance. The hose friction loss and nozzle pressure stay the same.
problems.explainMistake: Do not leave the pump at the ground-level setting; include the stated elevation allowance.
